## From two groups to three groups

With two groups, we saw that a linear regression model can reproduce the
two-sample t-test.

The same idea extends naturally to more than two groups.

Suppose we have three groups:

```{webr-r}
set.seed(1550)

dd <- data.table(
  group = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 50)
)

dd[, y := rnorm(
  .N,
  mean = fifelse(group == "A", 50,
         fifelse(group == "B", 55, 60)),
  sd = 10
)]

dd
```

We already know how to analyze these data using a one-way ANOVA:

```{webr-r}
fit_anova <- aov(y ~ group, data = dd)

summary(fit_anova)
```

The ANOVA asks whether the population means are all equal:

$$\large
H_0:\mu_A=\mu_B=\mu_C.
$$

Now let's analyze exactly the same data using linear regression:

```{webr-r}
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ group, data = dd)

tidy(fit_lm)
```

These may look like different analyses, but they are actually fitting the
same underlying linear model.

## How does regression represent three groups?

R uses one group as the **reference group**. Here, Group A is the reference.

The regression model can be written as

$$\large
E(Y \mid X)
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1 X_B
+
\beta_2 X_C,
$$

where

$$
X_B =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{Group B}\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad
X_C =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{Group C}\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

For Group A,

$$\large
E(Y\mid A)=\beta_0.
$$

For Group B,

$$\large
E(Y\mid B)=\beta_0+\beta_1.
$$

For Group C,

$$\large
E(Y\mid C)=\beta_0+\beta_2.
$$

So the regression coefficients have a simple interpretation:

- $\beta_0$ is the mean for **Group A**
- $\beta_1$ is the difference **B − A**
- $\beta_2$ is the difference **C − A**

We can see this directly by comparing the observed group means with the
regression coefficients:

```{webr-r}
dd[, .(mean_y = mean(y)), by = group]

coef(fit_lm)
```

The intercept gives the mean for Group A. Adding the appropriate coefficient
to the intercept gives the mean for Group B or Group C.

## Where did the ANOVA go?

The ANOVA null hypothesis was

$$\large
H_0:\mu_A=\mu_B=\mu_C.
$$

In the regression model, this is equivalent to

$$\large
H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0.
$$

If both coefficients are zero, neither Group B nor Group C differs from
Group A, so all three groups have the same mean.

We can ask R for an analysis-of-variance table for the regression model:

```{webr-r}
anova(fit_lm)
```

Compare this with the ANOVA we fit earlier:

```{webr-r}
summary(fit_anova)
```

The $F$ statistic and $p$-value are the same.

> **A one-way ANOVA is a linear regression model with a categorical predictor.**

## One potentially confusing R detail

The names of R's functions can make this connection less obvious.

`aov()` **fits a model**:

```{webr-r}
fit_anova <- aov(y ~ group, data = dd)
```

For this simple one-way ANOVA, `aov()` and `lm()` are fitting equivalent
linear models.

In contrast, `anova()` does **not** fit a model. It takes a model that has
already been fitted and produces an **analysis-of-variance table** for that
model:

```{webr-r}
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ group, data = dd)

anova(fit_lm)
```

So in the code above:

- `lm()` fits the linear model
- `anova()` produces the ANOVA table and $F$ test for that fitted model

The difference between the analyses we have called **ANOVA** and **linear
regression** is therefore not that they require fundamentally different
models. Instead, they give us different ways of looking at the same model.
